articles.title: How to Calculate Running Pace, Time and Distance
articles.excerpt: How running pace works, the formulas that link pace, time and distance, how to convert between minutes per kilometre and per mile, and finish times for 5K to a marathon.
blocks: Pace tells you how long it takes to cover one unit of distance, usually minutes per kilometre or minutes per mile. It is the number most runners use to plan a run or a race, because it stays the same whatever the distance. This guide gives the three formulas that link pace, time and distance, shows worked examples, explains how to switch between kilometres and miles, and lists the finish times that a given pace produces over the standard race distances. The Pace Calculator does these sums for you and shows each step.
Pace and speed are the same idea, turned upside down

Average speed is distance divided by time, so a speed of 10 km/h means ten kilometres every hour. Pace is the opposite way round: time divided by distance, so 6 minutes per kilometre means each kilometre takes six minutes. A faster runner has a higher speed and a lower pace number. You can convert between them: speed in km/h is 60 divided by the pace in minutes per kilometre, so 6:00 per km is 10 km/h.

Pace = Time ÷ Distance
Finish time = Pace × Distance
Distance = Time ÷ Pace
Always put the time into one unit first. Minutes and seconds are easiest to handle as total seconds, then turned back into minutes and seconds at the end.

A runner finishes 10 km in 55 minutes. That is 3,300 seconds. Pace = 3,300 ÷ 10 = 330 seconds per kilometre, which is 5 minutes 30 seconds, written 5:30 per km. In miles, one mile is exactly 1.609344 km, so 330 × 1.609344 = 531.1 seconds, which is 8:51 per mile. The speed is 3,600 ÷ 330 = 10.91 km/h.
Worked example 2: finding a finish time
A runner wants to hold 5:00 per km for a marathon. The marathon is 42.195 km, so the time is 300 × 42.195 = 12,658.5 seconds. That is 3 hours 30 minutes 58.5 seconds, about 3:30:59.
If you run for one hour at 6:00 per mile, the distance is 3,600 ÷ 360 = 10 miles, which is about 16.09 km.
The standard race distances are 5 km, 10 km, a half marathon of 21.0975 km and a marathon of 42.195 km. At a steady 5:30 per km the finish times are:

The calculator shows this table for whatever pace you enter. Real races are rarely run at one steady pace: hills, wind, crowds and tiredness all change it, so treat the table as a target, not a prediction.

Pace works backwards too. If you want to finish a 10 km race in 50 minutes, divide: 3,000 seconds ÷ 10 km = 300 seconds per km, which is 5:00 per km. Then check each kilometre against that number on the day. A simple approach is to write the target time for every kilometre or mile, 5:00, 10:00, 15:00 and so on, and see whether you are ahead or behind at each marker. Some runners start a little slower than the target and speed up, which is called a negative split. The calculator helps with the arithmetic, and the pace and speed shown together let you compare with a treadmill, which usually shows speed in km/h rather than pace.

Writing 5:30 as 5.30. Thirty seconds is half a minute, so 5:30 is 5.5 minutes, not 5.3
Mixing kilometres and miles, such as a pace per mile with a distance in kilometres
Using the pace for a short run to predict a marathon: pace usually slows as distance grows
Forgetting that stopping time, such as at a traffic light, is part of the elapsed time but not of the moving pace

Choose whether to find the pace, the finish time or the distance, then fill in the two values you know. The answer appears at the top, with the pace in both units, the speed, the race times, and a How this is calculated panel that writes out every step with your numbers.

articles.title: How to Add and Subtract Time: Hours, Minutes, Seconds
articles.excerpt: How to add and subtract hours, minutes and seconds by hand, when to carry and borrow, how to turn a total into days, and why 1:45 is not 1.45 hours.
blocks: Adding and subtracting time works like ordinary arithmetic, except that the units roll over at 60 and 24 instead of 10. That is why 45 minutes plus 30 minutes is 1 hour 15 minutes, not 75 hours. This guide shows how to add and subtract times by hand, how to carry and borrow between units, and how to avoid the usual slips. The Time Calculator does the same sums and shows its steps.

An hour is 60 minutes, which is exactly 3,600 seconds, and a day is 24 hours. The second is the SI base unit of time, and the minute, hour and day are the larger units built from it. So 1 day is 86,400 seconds, and any length of time can be written as a single number of seconds.
Line up the units and add each column, starting with the seconds. When a column reaches 60 (or 24 for hours), carry the extra into the next column.

Example: 2 h 45 min 30 s plus 1 h 30 min 50 s. Seconds: 30 + 50 = 80, which is 1 minute 20 seconds, so write 20 and carry 1 minute. Minutes: 45 + 30 + 1 = 76, which is 1 hour 16 minutes, so write 16 and carry 1 hour. Hours: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. The total is 4 h 16 min 20 s.
Subtracting by hand: borrow from the next unit

When the top number in a column is smaller, borrow one from the next unit up: 1 hour becomes 60 minutes, and 1 minute becomes 60 seconds. Example: 3 h 00 min minus 1 h 15 min. Minutes: 0 is less than 15, so borrow 1 hour (60 minutes): 60 − 15 = 45. Hours: 2 − 1 = 1. The answer is 1 h 45 min.

Turn each time into seconds, add or subtract, then turn the result back. For the first example, 2 h 45 min 30 s is 7,200 + 2,700 + 30 = 9,930 seconds, and 1 h 30 min 50 s is 3,600 + 1,800 + 50 = 5,450 seconds. The sum is 15,380 seconds. Divide by 3,600 to get 4 hours with 980 seconds left, which is 16 minutes 20 seconds. The answer matches. This is the method the calculator uses, because it works for any number of days, hours, minutes and seconds.

If you subtract a longer time from a shorter one, the result is negative: the first time is that much short of the second. The calculator shows the amount with a minus sign. For example, 10 minutes minus 25 minutes is −15 minutes.
Hours and minutes versus decimal hours

A time such as 1:45 means 1 hour and 45 minutes, which is 1.75 hours, because 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour. It is not 1.45 hours. To convert minutes to a decimal, divide by 60: 20 minutes is 0.333 hours and 30 minutes is 0.5 hours. To go back, multiply the decimal part by 60: 0.25 hours is 15 minutes.
Adding a longer list of times

With more than two times, add them one pair at a time, or convert every time to seconds and add them all at once. For example, three tracks of 3:45, 4:10 and 5:05 add up like this: 3:45 + 4:10 = 7:55, and 7:55 + 5:05 = 13:00. The same method gives the length of a playlist, the total of several lap times, or the total hours on a timesheet. If the total passes 60 minutes it becomes hours, and past 24 hours it becomes days, so a 100-hour total is 4 days and 4 hours.

Treating the minutes column like a decimal and carrying at 100 instead of 60
Forgetting to carry the extra minute from the seconds column
Reading 1:45 as 1.45 hours
Subtracting minutes without borrowing an hour first

The calculator accepts days, hours, minutes and seconds for each time, shows the answer in days, hours, minutes and seconds, and also gives the total in hours, minutes and seconds. The How this is calculated panel writes out each step.

articles.title: How to Calculate Hours Worked and Pay From Times
articles.excerpt: How to work out hours worked from a start and end time, subtract a break, handle a shift past midnight, convert minutes to decimal hours and multiply by a rate.
blocks: To find out how many hours someone worked, subtract the start time from the end time, then take off any unpaid break. To turn that into pay, convert the hours to a decimal and multiply by the hourly rate. This guide shows each step with examples, including shifts that end after midnight, and lists the slips that most often give the wrong total. The Hours Calculator does the sums and shows the working.

Hours worked = End time − Start time − Break
Decimal hours = Minutes ÷ 60
Pay = Hours worked × Hourly rate
Use a 24-hour clock to avoid confusion between morning and evening. An hour has 60 minutes, so work in minutes and divide by 60 at the end.

A shift runs from 09:00 to 17:30 with a 30-minute break. From 09:00 to 17:30 is 8 hours 30 minutes, which is 510 minutes. Take off the 30-minute break: 480 minutes, which is 8 hours exactly. Over 5 days that is 40 hours.
A shift that ends after midnight

If the end time is earlier than the start time, the shift crossed midnight. Add 24 hours (1,440 minutes) to the end time before subtracting. A shift from 22:00 to 06:00 is (6 × 60 + 1,440) − (22 × 60) = 1,800 − 1,320 = 480 minutes, which is 8 hours.

Pay is usually worked out with decimal hours, so 7 hours 30 minutes becomes 7.5 hours (30 ÷ 60 = 0.5). A few common conversions are 15 minutes = 0.25 hours, 20 minutes = 0.333 hours, 45 minutes = 0.75 hours. Do not write 7 hours 30 minutes as 7.30: that would read as 7 hours and 18 minutes.

Suppose the pay rate is ₹250 an hour. With 8 hours a day for 5 days, the total is 40 hours, and 40 × 250 = ₹10,000. If the day is 7 hours 45 minutes, that is 7.75 hours, so one day is 7.75 × 250 = ₹1,937.50.

If a break is paid, it counts as work time, so enter 0 minutes for the break. Only an unpaid break is taken off. Example: a worker starts at 08:30, finishes at 16:45 and takes an unpaid 45-minute break. From 08:30 to 16:45 is 8 hours 15 minutes. Take off 45 minutes and the day is 7 hours 30 minutes, which is 7.5 hours. Over 5 days that is 37.5 hours, and at ₹300 an hour the total is 37.5 × 300 = ₹11,250. For a week with different shifts each day, work out each day separately and add the decimal hours together, because adding hours and minutes by hand is where most slips happen.

The calculation counts clock time only. It does not apply overtime rates, rounding rules, paid breaks, night-shift extras, holidays, tax or other deductions. Employers and contracts follow their own rules on these, so check your contract or ask your employer before relying on a figure for pay. This is general information, not payroll or legal advice.

Forgetting to subtract the break
Ignoring that a shift crossed midnight, which gives a negative or very small answer
Entering 7 hours 30 minutes as 7.30 instead of 7.5
Mixing 12-hour and 24-hour times, so 5 in the afternoon is entered as 05:00 instead of 17:00

In the calculator, choose the start and end times, enter the break in minutes and the number of days, and add an hourly rate if you want the pay. The result shows the hours each day in hours and minutes and as a decimal, the total hours, and the pay, with every step in the How this is calculated panel. The second is the SI base unit of time and an hour is 3,600 seconds, so the calculator works in minutes and converts at the end.

articles.title: How to Add or Subtract Days, Months and Years to a Date
articles.excerpt: How to add or subtract days, weeks, months and years to a date, what happens at month ends, how leap years change the answer, and how to find the weekday.
blocks: Adding days to a date sounds simple until a month ends or a leap year gets in the way. This guide explains how to add or subtract days, weeks, months and years, what to do when a month is shorter than the start day, how leap years change the result, and the common mistakes. The Date Calculator follows the same rules and writes out each step.

Days are counted straight along the calendar, moving into the next month as needed. A week is exactly 7 days, so 2 weeks is 14 days. Example: 9 November 2026 plus 15 days. November has 30 days, so 9 + 15 = 24, and the result is 24 November 2026, a Tuesday. Counting back works the same way: 9 November minus 9 days is 31 October.

A month is not a fixed number of days, so months are added by moving the month number. Three months after 9 November 2026 is 9 February 2027. A year is 12 months, so 9 November 2026 plus 1 year is 9 November 2027. Adding one month is not the same as adding 30 days, because months have 28, 29, 30 or 31 days.

If the start day does not exist in the target month, the usual rule is to use the last day of that month. 31 January 2026 plus 1 month would be 31 February, which does not exist, so the answer is 28 February 2026. The calculator uses this rule and tells you when it applies.

A leap year adds a 29th day to February to keep the calendar in step with the solar year. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years, which must also be divisible by 400. So 2024 and 2000 are leap years, while 1900 and 2100 are not. The extra day is added because the Earth takes about 365 days and nearly 6 hours to go once round the Sun.

This changes answers. 28 February 2024 plus 1 day is 29 February 2024, but 28 February 2025 plus 1 day is 1 March 2025. 29 February 2024 plus 1 year has no 29 February in 2025, so the result is 28 February 2025.

When you add years, months, weeks and days together, add the years and months first, then the days. The calculator does it in that order, so 31 January plus 1 month and 3 days gives 28 February, then 3 March. Doing the days first would give a different answer.

A week has 7 days, so the weekday of the new date moves by the number of days added, modulo 7. Adding 15 days moves the weekday on by 1 (15 = 2 × 7 + 1), so a Monday becomes a Tuesday. The calculator shows the weekday of the result.

Ninety days from 1 January 2026 is 1 April 2026, because January has 31 days, February 28 and March 31, which together make exactly 90. Six weeks after 9 November 2026 is 21 December 2026: 6 weeks is 42 days, and 9 November plus 42 days lands on the same weekday, a Monday. Subtracting works the same way in reverse, so 6 months before 9 November 2026 is 9 May 2026. These patterns are useful for notice periods, subscription renewals, delivery estimates and project plans, as long as the document you are following counts days the same way.

Treating a month as 30 days
Forgetting that February has 29 days in a leap year
Adding the days before the months when both are given
Not checking the date before using it for something that matters, such as a legal deadline, where the rules for counting days may be set by the document or the law

Enter a start date, choose add or subtract, and fill in any of years, months, weeks and days. The calculator shows the resulting date, its weekday, how many days away it is, and the steps. Dates run from the year 1900 to 2200.
